newsitem.title: UK: Oil price eases with milder US weather outlook.
newsitem.headline: Oil price eases with milder US weather outlook.

text.p: Oil prices were weaker on Monday as weather forecasters predicted warmer temperatures in the United States than had earlier been expected, traders at London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) said on Monday.

IPE February futures for benchmark North Sea Brent crude blend closed 26 cents a barrel down on the day at $23.20 and dealers said the weather-related weakness in U.S. futures markets was the main force driving London prices lower.
"Fundamentally, the pressure has come from New York," one IPE floor trader said.

But activity ahead of the Christmas holiday was pitifully thin and the disgruntled trader summed up the lack of activity thus: "It has been a horrible market and a complete waste of time today as far as I am concerned."

Private forecasters Weather Services Corp. said temperatures in the key heating oil markets of the northeastern United States on Monday and Tuesday were expected to average six to 15 degrees above normal and to average near normal through Friday.

In Vienna, the secretariat of the Organisation for Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) admitted for the first time on Monday that over half a million barrels per day (bpd) of extra Iraqi oil, now flooding onto world markets under a renewable $2 billion oil-for-food deal with the U.N., would exert downwards pressure on oil prices.

The report contrasts with recent statements from the oil ministers of various OPEC countries, who have argued that world oil markets can take Iraq's oil in their stride because of surging winter demand and historically low inventories.
The OPEC report forecast a contraseasonal 500-600,000 bpd build in world oil stocks during the first quarter of next year.
"The implication of this would be downwards pressure on prices during the first quarter of 1997 and possibly for the remainder of the year," the report added.

But despite the oil-for-food deal, sanctions imposed in 1990 when Iraq invaded Kuwait remain in force and there is little prospect of them being lifted in the immediate future, diplomatic sources say.
Traders said news that Iraq and international oil companies were continuing to sign fresh marketing contracts, so far worth 551,000 barrels per day (bpd,) failed to have an impact on prices.
Iraq's first exports in six years of U.N. sanctions set sail a week ago.
